Three Knots Worth Knowing
A good camper carries a torch, a water bottle and a length of rope. But a rope is only as useful as the knots you can tie in it. Learn these three, and you will be ready for almost anything the bush throws at you.
The reef knot
The reef knot joins two ends of rope together. It is perfect for tying up a bundle of firewood or closing the top of a bag. To tie it, remember 'right over left, then left over right'. A reef knot lies flat and neat, but be careful: it can slip loose if it is pulled very hard, so never use it to hold anything heavy.
The bowline
The bowline (say 'BOH-lin') makes a loop at the end of a rope that will not shrink or slip, no matter how much weight hangs from it. Sailors have trusted it for hundreds of years. Best of all, even after holding a heavy load, a bowline is easy to undo.
The taut-line hitch
This clever knot is a tent's best friend. Tie it where a guy rope loops around a tent peg. It can slide along the rope to tighten or loosen it, yet it grips firmly when the rope is pulled. Ropes often stretch when they get wet, and a sagging tent can collect puddles on its roof overnight. With a taut-line hitch, you simply slide the knot to make the rope tight again.
Why not grab a piece of string tonight and start practising?

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
When Stories Come True
Science fiction writers imagine what the future might look like. Sometimes, their wild ideas turn out to be surprisingly close to the truth.
More than 150 years ago, the French writer Jules Verne described a trip to the Moon. In his story, the travellers launched from Florida, felt weightless in space and splashed down in the ocean on their return. About a hundred years later, real astronauts did almost exactly that.
In 1945, a young British writer named Arthur C. Clarke suggested placing machines high above Earth to send radio signals around the world. People thought it sounded far-fetched. Today, communication satellites carry television, phone calls and internet signals across the planet every second.
Even the word 'robot' came from fiction. It first appeared in a play written in 1920 by a Czech writer.
Some inventors say these stories inspired them. As a boy, Igor Sikorsky read a different Jules Verne novel, featuring a flying machine that could rise straight up into the air. He never forgot it. Decades later, he designed one of the first successful helicopters.
Of course, many predictions have not come true. We are still waiting for flying cars to fill our skies! But science fiction does something important. It encourages us to ask 'What if?' In my opinion, that question is the most exciting one there is.

AnswerB: 'the word 'robot' came from fiction'
AnswerC: 'that question is the most exciting one there is'
AnswerD: 'he designed one of the first successful helicopters'

ComprehensionText:
Maria Montessori's Small Chairs
Maria Montessori was born in Italy in 1870. At a time when most girls were expected to stay at home, Maria wanted to study science. Some people made fun of her, but she refused to give up. In 1896, she became one of the first women in Italy to qualify as a doctor.
As a doctor, Maria worked with children who were struggling to learn. She watched them closely and noticed that they learned best when they could touch and move things with their hands, rather than sitting still and listening.
In 1907, Maria opened a school for young children in a poor part of Rome. She called it the Casa dei Bambini, which means 'Children's House'. Most classrooms then had heavy desks bolted to the floor in rows. Maria's classroom was different. She had small, light tables and chairs made that children could carry themselves. Shelves were low, so children could reach things without asking an adult.
Children chose their own activities, such as pouring water, building towers of blocks or tracing letters cut from sandpaper. Visitors were amazed to see three- and four-year-olds working quietly for long periods.
Maria spent the rest of her life travelling the world to share her ideas. Today, there are thousands of Montessori schools, and many other classrooms have child-sized furniture too.

AnswerA: painted brightly
AnswerB: fixed firmly
AnswerC: ran away quickly
AnswerD: pushed together
